title: Tambour stitch
subtitle: A hooked chain stitch pulled up through taut fabric from below
excerpt: Tambour stitch is chain stitch formed not with a needle but with a fine tambour hook, a small hook set in a handle much like a crochet hook. The fabric is stretched drum-tight in a tambour frame; the working thread is held below the frame while the hook descends through the fabric from above, catches the thread, and draws a loop up through the previous loop. The result is a continuous chain on the surface of the fabric, worked at speed.
sourceNotes: Thérèse de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886); Caulfeild & Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882).

glossaryTerms.definition: The length of thread currently being stitched with, running from the fabric to the needle.

content.text: Tambour stitch is a chain stitch technique that uses a fine hook rather than a needle. The

is fed from a bobbin or cone held under the fabric, out of sight. The hook operator works entirely from above the frame, plunging the hook tip down through the fabric, catching the thread below, and drawing a loop up through the loop already on the hook. Because the hook penetrates at a near-vertical angle and the thread never passes over the surface during formation, tambour can be worked far faster than needle chain stitch. It is the technique behind Lunéville embroidery and much traditional beaded couture work.

items.label: Thread
items.value: Fine continuous-filament thread such as silk twist or fine polyester; the thread must run freely from below without tangling

items.label: Fabric
items.value: Fine, tightly woven silk, net, or organdie; the fabric must be completely taut so the hook pierces cleanly without snagging

items.label: Needle
items.value: A tambour hook (a fine hook set in a pen-style handle, sized 80 to 100 for fine work); not a sewing needle

items.label: Hoop
items.value: A tambour frame or a very tight embroidery hoop, fabric stretched drum-tight; slack fabric makes the hook catch and tear

content.text: Stretch the fabric in the tambour frame until it is completely drum-tight. Secure the working thread below the fabric, holding it in your non-dominant hand under the frame so it feeds freely along the design line.
To start, bring the first loop up through the fabric by inserting the hook at point A and catching the thread below to draw a small loop to the surface. Hold this loop on the hook.
Move the hook a short distance along the design line to point B. The hook remains on the surface with the existing loop on it. Plunge the hook tip straight down through the fabric at B.

Below the frame, the hand holding the thread guides it into the path of the hook. Catch the thread with the hook tip and draw a new loop up through the fabric and through the loop already on the hook. The previous loop closes and locks around the new one, forming one chain link on the fabric surface.

Advance to point C and repeat. Each plunge-catch-draw creates one more link. The hook always enters from above; the thread always remains below. Keep the thread tension below consistent by letting it feed through your fingers at a steady rate.
To fasten off, draw the thread end up through the last loop. Take both this thread and the starting tail to the back with a needle. Secure them with a few small stitches.

items.symptom: The hook tears the fabric instead of piercing cleanly
items.cause: The fabric is not tight enough in the frame, or the hook size is too large for the fabric weave.
items.fix: Re-tension the fabric until it feels drum-tight. Use a finer hook for sheer or fine fabrics. The hook should slip through a single gap in the weave, not force one open.

items.symptom: The chain breaks or loops drop off
items.cause: The thread below the frame was allowed to run slack, or the hook rotated while plunging so the thread missed the hook tip.
items.fix: Keep the thread in the hand below taut and positioned directly along the design line. Hold the hook handle so the hook tip always faces in the direction of travel; do not let it twist.

items.symptom: Chain links are uneven in size
items.cause: The distance between plunge points varies, or the amount of thread drawn up per loop is inconsistent.
items.fix: Work at a slow, steady pace until the hand below and the hook above develop a consistent rhythm. Mark the design line clearly and keep plunge points equally spaced.
